title: Civil Liberties and Human Rights Movements

cards.h: Who defends rights against the State?
cards.b:
Constitutions promise rights, but the State itself can violate them through custodial torture, preventive detention, encounter killings or special security laws. Civil liberties and human rights movements are groups of citizens, lawyers and journalists who document such violations and fight them in courts and in public.

In India these movements were born out of the Emergency (1975-77), when over a lakh people were detained and the Supreme Court denied habeas corpus in ADM Jabalpur (1976).

Exam questions ask about their origin, achievements, the tension between security and liberty, and laws such as AFSPA, UAPA and the sedition provision.

• APDR (Association for Protection of Democratic Rights, West Bengal, 1972), formed in the wake of the Naxalite crackdown.
  • PUCL (People's Union for Civil Liberties): founded as the People's Union for Civil Liberties and Democratic Rights under J.P. Narayan's inspiration in 1976; reorganised as PUCL in 1980. Rajni Kothari was among its leaders.
  • PUDR (People's Union for Democratic Rights, Delhi): its 1984 report Who Are the Guilty? (with PUCL) documented the anti-Sikh violence.
  • Others: Naga People's Movement for Human Rights, Manipur's families' associations, Human Rights Law Network, and Amnesty International India (which halted operations in 2020 after its accounts were frozen).

Indian groups debated their focus:

  • Civil liberties approach (PUCL): defend liberal freedoms of all, against any State excess, without a class line.
  • Democratic rights approach (PUDR, APDR): rights are tied to the struggles of workers, peasants, tribals and Dalits; violations come from the structure of power, not just bad officials.

A.R. Desai (ed.), Violation of Democratic Rights in India (1986)

A Marxist sociologist's documentation of how the State's development model produced repression of the poor.

Upendra Baxi

Called for "social action litigation" and a human rights view grounded in suffering, in The Future of Human Rights (2002).

• ADM Jabalpur (1976): no habeas corpus during the Emergency; H.R. Khanna's dissent. Overruled in Puttaswamy (2017).
  • PIL era: Hussainara Khatoon (1979) on undertrials; Sunil Batra (1978) on prisoners' rights; Nilabati Behera (1993) on compensation for custodial death.
  • D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997): arrest guidelines (identification, memo, informing relatives, medical checks).
  • PUCL v. Union of India (1997): phone tapping limits; PUCL (2014) guidelines on encounter killings.
  • Extra-Judicial Execution Victim Families Association v. Union (2016): even in areas under AFSPA, excessive force is open to inquiry; Manipur encounter cases investigated.
  • Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down section 66A of the IT Act.
  • S.G. Vombatkere (May 2022): sedition (s.124A IPC) kept in abeyance. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (2023) dropped "sedition" but section 152 punishes acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity.

• AFSPA (1958): gives armed forces powers to shoot, arrest and search in "disturbed areas", with immunity from prosecution without central sanction. The Jeevan Reddy Committee (2005) recommended repeal. Irom Sharmila fasted against it from 2000 to 2016. AFSPA areas in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur were reduced from 2022.
  • UAPA (1967): amended in 2004, 2008, 2012 and 2019 (allowing individuals to be designated as terrorists). Bail is very hard (section 43D(5)); NIA v. Zahoor Watali (2019) made it stricter.
  • Preventive detention: Article 22 allows it; laws such as the National Security Act (1980) and state Public Safety Acts.
  • Internet shutdowns: Anuradha Bhasin (2020) required proportionality and publication of orders.

The State's case: India faces insurgencies, terrorism and Maoist violence; special laws are needed and rights groups sometimes ignore violence by armed groups.

The movements' case:

  • Low conviction rates under UAPA suggest misuse as process-as-punishment.
  • Custodial deaths and encounters continue; India has signed (1997) but not ratified the UN Convention against Torture.
  • Impunity under AFSPA erodes trust in border regions.

Critique of the movements: dependence on courts; urban, middle-class leadership; limited reach. Partha Chatterjee's distinction between civil society and political society suggests the poor often negotiate rights through politics rather than legal activism.

A balanced answer accepts both security and rights, and demands accountability: independent inquiry, quick trials, and review of special laws.

• Bhima Koregaon case (arrests from 2018): activists held under UAPA; Father Stan Swamy died in custody on 5 July 2021 while awaiting bail, at 84.
  • Manipur (2023-26): violence, internet shutdowns and the Supreme Court's committee of former judges.
  • Ladakh (September 2025): protests and the reported detention of Sonam Wangchuk under the National Security Act.
  • Kashmir after 2019: detentions and internet restrictions; Anuradha Bhasin (2020).
  • NHRC: GANHRI deferred its accreditation review in 2023-24.
  • New criminal laws (in force 1 July 2024) extended police custody options, which rights groups criticised.

• Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948); the two covenants of 1966 (ICCPR and ICESCR), which India ratified in 1979.
  • Three "generations": civil-political, socio-economic, and group rights (development, environment), a framework from Karel Vasak.
  • Cultural relativism and the "Asian values" debate of the 1990s.
  • In India, the Supreme Court has used international law to fill gaps (Vishaka, 1997).

"Discuss the role of civil liberties movements in Indian democracy."
"Security laws versus civil liberties: examine with reference to AFSPA and UAPA."
"Human rights movements in India have been largely urban and court-centred." Comment.

Structure: Emergency origin; organisations and their approaches; landmark cases; contested laws; critique on both sides; recent cases; conclude with accountability-based balance.
